title: Introduction to Probability
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 2.4 Introduction to Probability
intro: After this lesson you can list a sample space, find a probability from equally likely outcomes, use the complement rule, and avoid common errors with two-dice sums and the words "likely" and "unlikely".

moments.title: Sample space
moments.text: The set of all possible nonoverlapping outcomes. Its probability is 1.

moments.title: Equally likely outcomes
moments.text: $P(E)$ is the number of outcomes in $E$ divided by the number of outcomes in the sample space.

moments.title: $P(E)$ notation
moments.text: $P(E)$ means the probability of event $E$. It is not multiplication.

moments.title: Probability is between 0 and 1
moments.text: Inclusive of 0 and 1. A probability cannot be negative or exceed 1.

moments.title: Likely and unlikely are not at 50%
moments.text: A 45% chance is not unlikely. Unlikely usually means well below 5%.

moments.title: Complement of an event
moments.text: The probability that $E$ does not happen. Written $E^C$, $E^\prime$ or "not $E$".

moments.title: Probability is a long-run statement
moments.text: Ten rolls need not give exactly five odd numbers. The probability describes the long run.

moments.title: Two dice, sample space of 36
moments.text: There are $6\times6=36$ equally likely ordered outcomes.

moments.title: Sums are not equally likely
moments.text: The 36 ordered pairs are equally likely, but the sums 2 to 12 are not.

moments.title: Sum of seven
moments.text: Six of 36 pairs give a sum of 7, so $P=6/36=1/6$.

moments.title: Sum of at most five
moments.text: "At most five" means 5 or less. Ten of 36 outcomes qualify.

moments.title: Grade and eye color table
moments.text: Out of 850 students, 220 are in grade 10, 110 have green eyes, and 45 are seniors with blue eyes.

moments.title: Marbles in a jar
moments.text: 5 red, 7 green and 3 yellow. The colors are not equally likely, but the 15 marbles are.

sections.title: Can I use favorable over total?

cards.name: Equally likely
cards.text: Each listed outcome has the same chance, so count favorable outcomes over total outcomes.

cards.name: Not equally likely
cards.text: List the equally likely outcomes underneath, such as the 36 dice pairs, then count.

cells: Faces 1 to 6 on a fair die
Colors red, green, yellow in a jar of 5, 7 and 3
A student chosen at random from 850

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The video says the answer to "unlikely" has no 50% cutoff. Use the numbers: a 28% event is not rare, and an event is called unlikely only when its probability is quite small.

sections.title: Calculate a probability and its complement
sections.intro: List outcomes that are equally likely, count the favorable ones, then use the complement when "not" is easier.
steps: Decide what the equally likely outcomes are and how many there are.
Count the outcomes in the event. Read words such as at most carefully.
Divide, then answer in context. Use $1-P(E)$ for "not $E$".

traps.title: Treating dice sums as equally likely
traps.weak: The sums 2 to 12 are 11 outcomes, so each has probability $1/11$.
traps.better: The 36 ordered pairs are equally likely. A sum of 7 has 6 pairs, so $P=6/36$, while a sum of 12 has 1 pair, so $P=1/36$.

traps.title: Treating colors as equally likely
traps.better: There are 15 equally likely marbles and 5 are red, so $P(\text{red})=5/15=1/3$. The answer is only 1/3 because 5 of 15 is 1/3.

traps.title: At most means less than or equal
traps.weak: At most 5 means the sums 2, 3 and 4.
traps.better: At most 5 means 5 or less: sums of 2, 3, 4 and 5, which is 10 of 36 outcomes.

traps.title: Probability read as a short-run promise
traps.weak: The probability of an odd number is 1/2, so ten rolls give exactly five odd numbers.
traps.better: The probability 1/2 describes the long-run relative frequency. Ten rolls may give any number of odd results.

traps.title: Using 50% as the cutoff for unlikely
traps.weak: A 40% chance is unlikely because it is below one half.
traps.better: A 40% chance is not unlikely. Describe an event as unlikely only when its probability is close to 0.

questions.stem: A bag contains 8 blue, 7 white and 5 black tiles, all the same size. One tile is chosen at random. What is $P(\text{not white})$?
why: Treating the three colors as equally likely is the mistake.

questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled. Which sum is most likely?
why: Equal likelihood holds for the 36 pairs, not for the sums.
Only the pair 1 and 1 gives a sum of 2.
Correct. Six of the 36 ordered pairs give a sum of 7.
Only the pair 6 and 6 gives a sum of 12.

questions.stem: Which value could be a probability?
why: Correct. 0 is allowed and means the event is impossible.

questions.stem: The probability of rain tomorrow is 0.10. Which statement is correct?
opts: The probability of no rain is 0.90.
It will rain on 1 of the next 10 days.
why: Correct. The complement of rain has probability $1-0.10$.
A probability of 0.10 does not guarantee that it will not rain.
Probability describes long-run frequencies, not a guaranteed pattern in the next 10 days.
No rain has probability 0.90, which is likely.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A student rolls two fair six-sided dice and records the larger of the two numbers (if they match, that number).
parts: (a) List the sample space of equally likely outcomes and state how many there are.
(c) Find the probability that the larger number is not 6.
(d) Explain why 11 equally likely outcomes would be the wrong sample space for the larger number.
sample: (a) The 36 ordered pairs (first die, second die) are equally likely.
(b) 11 pairs contain at least one 6, so $P=0.306$.
(d) The larger number takes values 1 to 6, which are not equally likely. For example, the larger number is 1 in only one pair but 6 in eleven pairs.
checklist: (d) Explains outcomes are not equally likely
